title: Chiggers: The Phantom Menace
summary: Josh and Chuck explore chiggers, the larvae of harvest mites (arachnids, not insects). They explain that chiggers do not burrow or suck blood; instead they inject saliva that liquefies skin cells, and their surrounding skin hardens into a feeding tube called a stylostome. The hosts cover where chiggers hang out on the body, their light and temperature sensitivity, their questing behavior, the typhus risk from one species in Asia, and home remedies (nail polish, turpentine, anti-itch cream) versus prevention. They also cover a paper-on-the-ground method for detecting chiggers. Includes tangents on other blood-feeding pests, a fitness club announcement, and a listener mail about dental and nasal injections.

segments.title: Opening banter and chigger setup
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the chigger topic as suggested by Tracy Wilson's article, joke about poison ivy, and Josh sets up common misconceptions about chiggers.

segments.title: Chiggers are not insects: harvest mite larvae
segments.summary: Chiggers are the larvae of harvest mites, which are arachnids related to spiders. The larvae have six legs before growing their adult legs. Adults eat eggs of pests like mosquitoes. Harvest mite females lay eggs in one spot, so chiggers cluster in patches of yard.

segments.title: The chigger's first meal and why it doesn't burrow
segments.summary: Newly hatched larvae need one complete meal to develop further. Chiggers do not burrow into skin; they attach briefly and are usually scratched off, so the meal is often never completed. Most hosts are not their preferred prey, and they feed on many vertebrates.

segments.title: Chigger hosts, Asian typhus risk, and the chigger's senses
segments.summary: Only one species, Leptotrombidium delicense, is a serious human threat, carrying typhus in parts of Asia. Chiggers seek shade, respond to shadows and body heat, and use touch-sensitive hairs. They hide in warm, protected spots like the back of the knee, armpits, and waistbands, and climb to high points to wait in a questing posture.

segments.title: Digestive saliva, stylostome feeding tube, and itch
segments.summary: Chiggers inject saliva that breaks down skin cells into a slurry. The surrounding tissue hardens into a temporary tube called a stylostome, which the chigger drinks through. The lingering tube causes the persistent itch as skin heals, and the itch is worse with longer feeding.

segments.title: Treating chigger bites and home remedies
segments.summary: The hosts discuss home remedies like nail polish, which protects the wound from air rather than suffocating a chigger, and warn against turpentine and digging out the stylostome. Tracy recommends anti-itch cream such as cortisone. They also explain the name confusion with jigger fleas, which do burrow and lay eggs.

segments.title: Chigger prevention and paper-on-stick test
segments.summary: Prevention includes wearing long sleeves and pants and using insect repellent; sulfur is also mentioned. Tracy suggests standing black paper on its edge in grass to see whether chiggers climb it, which the hosts doubt works. Keeping the yard maintained reduces chiggers.

segments.title: Fitness club announcement
segments.summary: Josh promotes a stuff you should know listener fitness group on the MyFitnessPal app.

segments.title: Listener mail: injection stories
segments.summary: A listener named Julie from Honolulu shares a story about a painful root canal injection and mentions the hosts' earlier episode on anesthesia, including a Harvard student's nasal numbing injections.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close with social media and website information and a pointer to HowStuffWorks.com for more on chiggers.
